package_info.package_name: N/A (RepoJacking is a technique, not a specific package)
package_info.package_manager: GitHub (affects Go, Swift, PHP, and any language pulling code from GitHub)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects all versions of repos vulnerable to RepoJacking)
package_info.why_malicious: RepoJacking enables attackers to take over popular repository namespaces after a username rename, allowing them to publish malicious code under trusted package names. This poisons the software supply chain by serving malicious code to users and applications that depend on the hijacked repositories, leading to potential credential theft, data exfiltration, and compromise of downstream systems.

execution_context.file_location: main.go (or equivalent entrypoint in hijacked repo)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code accesses the SECRET_TOKEN environment variable, sends its value to a hardcoded external domain via HTTPS POST, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code reads a sensitive environment variable (SECRET_TOKEN) and immediately transmits it to an external server controlled by the attacker, which is a clear sign of malicious exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate open-source packages do not access or transmit environment variables, especially secrets, during import or build time, nor do they make unsolicited network requests in initialization code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or error reporting libraries may send anonymized usage data, but they never transmit secrets or tokens without explicit user consent.
key_indicators: Access to sensitive environment variables (e.g., SECRET_TOKEN)
Hardcoded external domain (https://attacker.com/exfil) for data exfiltration
Network requests initiated at import/build time
Use of init() function for automatic execution

execution_context.file_location: Package.swift (or equivalent entrypoint in hijacked Swift repo)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads the API_KEY environment variable, posts its value to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain via HTTP POST, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is designed to extract a sensitive environment variable (API_KEY) and send it to an external server, which is a direct violation of expected package behavior and a hallmark of credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not access or exfiltrate secrets such as API keys during import or build, nor do they make network requests to unknown domains without user action.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases for exfiltrating secrets to hardcoded domains at import/build time; this is a clear abuse.
key_indicators: Access to environment variables (API_KEY) in initialization code
Execution of network requests at import/build time
Use of URLSession for unsolicited data transmission

attack_chain.action: Attacker claims a GitHub username that was previously renamed by a popular package maintainer.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to create a repository with the same name as the original, trusted package.

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as the original, trusted package under the hijacked username.
attack_chain.leads_to: Hijacked repository is now available at the original namespace, making it indistinguishable from the legitimate source for automated tooling.

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes malicious code in the hijacked repository (e.g., credential exfiltration code).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is served to users and applications that import the package via GitHub URL, enabling supply chain compromise.

attack_chain.action: Victims import or build the package, triggering execution of the malicious code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive data (e.g., tokens, API keys) to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected network requests initiated during import/build time in package initialization code
Access to sensitive environment variables (e.g., SECRET_TOKEN, API_KEY) in entrypoint files
Code that posts data to hardcoded external domains (e.g., attacker.com) during package initialization
file_indicators: main.go, Package.swift, or other entrypoint files containing network exfiltration logic
Sudden changes in repository code or behavior after a username rename or namespace takeover
Presence of init() functions or global code blocks that perform network operations
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., https://attacker.com/exfil, https://attacker.com/steal) from build/import processes
New or unrecognized domains contacted by package initialization code
Unusual network activity originating from build servers or CI pipelines
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose repository namespace has recently changed ownership, especially following a username rename. Flag packages that make network requests or access environment variables during import/build by using static analysis to detect hardcoded external domains and suspicious data flows in entrypoint files. Alert on any package that suddenly changes behavior or codebase after a namespace takeover. Correlate network telemetry to identify outbound connections to attacker-controlled domains from build or import processes.
